overview: Entergy is a Fortune 500 vertically integrated electric utility holding company serving roughly 3 million customers in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and the City of New Orleans through its regulated subsidiaries (Entergy Arkansas, Entergy Louisiana, Entergy Mississippi, Entergy New Orleans, Entergy Texas) plus System Energy, which owns a 90% interest in the Grand Gulf nuclear plant. The company generates, transmits, and distributes electric power from a generation fleet that includes nuclear, natural gas, and renewable assets, and it exited natural gas distribution in July 2025 by selling that business to Delta Utilities (Bernhard Capital Partners). Entergy operates as a single reportable segment (Utility), with a small non-utility Parent & Other category.

business_model.summary: Entergy earns regulated returns on rate base by generating, transmitting, and distributing electricity to residential, commercial, industrial, and governmental customers under cost-of-service regulation set by state commissions (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas) and the New Orleans City Council, plus FERC oversight of wholesale/transmission. Revenue is largely non-discretionary and recurring, driven by allowed ROE on an expanding rate base (now growing rapidly on data-center-driven capital spending) rather than by volume growth alone, since fuel/purchased power costs are largely passed through to customers.
business_model.customer_type: Regulated B2C (residential), B2B commercial and large industrial (including hyperscale data centers), and wholesale/municipal customers
business_model.geographic_mix: Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and the City of New Orleans (Gulf South); FY2025 Utility operating revenues were approximately $12.9 billion

competitive_position.market_position: Regulated monopoly electric utility in its Gulf South service territories; not in direct retail competition but competes with peer regulated utilities for capital, large-load customer siting decisions (data centers, industrial), and regulatory/legislative favor

moat_factors.description: Exclusive service territories granted by state commissions create a legal monopoly on transmission and distribution within its footprint
Electricity is a non-discretionary service with no practical substitute for most customers, supporting stable, inelastic demand

Large nuclear (Grand Gulf, River Bend, Waterford 3, Arkansas Nuclear One) and gas generation base provides low-carbon and dispatchable capacity attractive to data-center customers seeking reliable, 24/7 power

moat_factors.factor: First-mover position in Gulf South data-center siting
moat_factors.description: Large, contracted agreements with Meta and Google and a 7-12 GW pipeline of additional data-center interest give Entergy a head start in capturing hyperscale load in a historically low-growth footprint

weaknesses: Geographic concentration in a few state regulatory jurisdictions (Louisiana, Mississippi, Arkansas, Texas) exposes earnings to a small number of commissions' decisions
High hurricane/storm exposure along the Gulf Coast creates large, lumpy capital and O&M needs subject to recovery risk and timing lag
Aging nuclear fleet (Grand Gulf, River Bend) has a history of unplanned outages and NRC scrutiny
Elevated leverage and a rapidly growing, multi-year capital program create execution and financing risk, including reliance on equity issuance and hybrid debt
Lower household income levels in parts of its service territory limit retail rate-increase tolerance versus wealthier utility territories

growth_drivers: Data-center and large industrial load growth: management's pipeline spans roughly 7-12 GW of data-center interest plus 3-5 GW of other industrial discussions, with contracted agreements already signed with Meta (West Memphis-area combined-cycle/battery buildout) and an expanded Google agreement for a West Memphis data-center campus

Multi-year capital investment plan that has grown from roughly $37-43 billion (2026-2029) to over $50 billion including the Meta-driven increase, directly expanding rate base and driving >8% targeted annual EPS growth through 2030

New natural gas combined-cycle generation and battery storage build-out to serve large new industrial/data-center loads under long-term contracts that include customer protections (minimum take agreements, credit support)
Transmission and distribution investment (~$17 billion of the 2026-2029 plan) to support grid reliability, resilience, and interconnection of new large loads
Continued industrial reshoring/petrochemical and LNG-adjacent growth in the Gulf South region supporting the non-data-center industrial base
Portfolio simplification following the 2025 sale of the natural gas distribution business, sharpening focus and capital allocation toward the core regulated electric utility

business.risk: Customer/load concentration in large data-center and industrial contracts
business.description: A growing share of load growth depends on a relatively small number of hyperscale customers (e.g., Meta, Google); contract cancellation, delay, or AI capex slowdown could leave Entergy with stranded-asset risk
Grand Gulf and River Bend have histories of unplanned outages and NRC scrutiny; an extended outage removes significant baseload capacity and can increase purchased-power costs
Gulf Coast footprint is highly exposed to hurricanes and storms that can cause major infrastructure damage and require large restoration costs

financial.risk: Elevated leverage amid a rapidly growing capex program
financial.description: Multi-year capital plan now exceeds $50 billion; funding requires substantial new debt and equity issuance (including hybrid/junior subordinated debentures), pressuring credit metrics (FFO-to-debt) and diluting EPS
As a capital-intensive, debt-funded utility, Entergy's financing costs and valuation multiple are sensitive to the level of long-term interest rates
Securitization and rate-case recovery of storm restoration costs can lag actual spend, creating working-capital and regulatory-lag risk

regulatory.description: Earnings depend on timely, adequate rate relief from the Louisiana PSC, Mississippi PSC, Arkansas PSC, Public Utility Commission of Texas, New Orleans City Council, and FERC; any commission could disallow costs or limit allowed ROE

regulatory.risk: Large-load tariff design and cost-allocation disputes
regulatory.description: As data-center contracts scale, regulators and consumer advocates are scrutinizing whether residential/commercial customers are adequately protected from stranded-cost or cross-subsidization risk
NRC oversight of aging nuclear units carries compliance costs and potential for extended outages or relicensing conditions
EPA rules on emissions, coal/gas ash, and water use affect generation fleet costs and timelines for new gas-fired capacity additions

macro.description: Entergy's growth thesis is now closely tied to continued hyperscaler data-center investment; a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending would reduce incremental load growth

macro.risk: Natural gas and commodity price exposure
macro.description: Fuel costs are largely passed through to customers, limiting direct margin risk, but sustained high prices can pressure customer bills and political/regulatory tolerance for rate increases
Lower-income service territory and industrial customer base (petrochemicals, refining) make retail and industrial sales somewhat sensitive to regional economic cycles

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated electric utilities are experiencing the strongest load-growth outlook in decades, driven by data centers/AI, industrial reshoring, and electrification; Entergy's Gulf South footprint has become a focal point for hyperscale data-center siting due to available land, gas infrastructure, and utility willingness to structure large-load tariffs
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate; regulated utility earnings are largely non-cyclical and demand is inelastic, though industrial/petrochemical customer volumes have some economic sensitivity and storm costs create earnings volatility
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High; utility valuations and financing costs for its large capital program are sensitive to long-term rates, and the sector trades as a bond-proxy
key_input_costs: Construction/commodity costs for new gas and battery capacity
Labor/contractor costs for the capital program

recent_developments.event: Reported Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.98 (vs. $1.53 prior year); narrowed FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $4.35-$4.45 (low end raised from $4.25); reaffirmed >8% annual EPS growth target through 2030

Expanded agreement with Google for the West Memphis-area data-center campus, expected to generate at least $500 million in additional Arkansas customer bill savings; data-center pipeline held at 7-12 GW with 3-5 GW of additional industrial interest

Increased planned capital spending for 2027-2030 by roughly $1.5 billion, with the 2027-2030 construction plan reported near $54.7 billion, including $17.2 billion for 2027; industrial sales growth moderated to 4.9% from ~10% in Q2 and ~15% in Q1

Signed a major agreement with Meta tied to a West Memphis-area data-center campus involving seven new combined-cycle gas units and battery storage; raised the four-year capital plan by roughly $14 billion as a result
Completed equity issuance (~$2.2 billion, May 2026) and two $750 million fixed-to-floating junior subordinated debenture offerings (due 2056/2058) to help fund the expanded capital program
Raised the 2026-2029 capital plan by $2 billion to roughly $43 billion, including $11.6 billion for 2026 and about $17 billion earmarked for transmission and distribution

Completed the sale of its natural gas distribution business (Entergy Louisiana and Entergy New Orleans gas operations, ~95,000 and ~109,000 customers respectively) to Delta Utilities, backed by Bernhard Capital Partners, sharpening focus on the core regulated electric utility

items.notes: Low end raised by $0.10 from prior range of $4.25-$4.45
Management said incremental capital spending moves Entergy toward the upper half of its 2027-2030 earnings outlook ranges
Increased by approximately $1.5 billion in Q3 2026; builds on an earlier $43 billion 2026-2029 plan that itself had been raised ~$14 billion after the Meta agreement

items.target: 7-12 GW data center, 3-5 GW other industrial (plus up to 17 GW of additional opportunities under discussion)
items.notes: Pipeline range held steady quarter-over-quarter; 23 GW (31 natural gas plants) now in the generation development queue
Industrial sales growth slowed from ~10% in Q2 2026 and ~15% in Q1 2026 as comparisons normalized

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Drew Marsh emphasized continued confidence in the data-center and industrial load pipeline and in financing the expanded capital program while protecting customers through minimum-take and credit-support contract structures; management reiterated it is not yet including unsigned pipeline opportunities or new nuclear in its base capital plan, citing cost and risk uncertainty on nuclear new-build.

bull_case: Rare, multi-decade load-growth inflection driven by contracted hyperscale data-center demand (Meta, Google) in a historically slow-growth Gulf South service territory, directly expanding regulated rate base
Visible, growing capital investment plan (now ~$50+ billion through 2029/2030) provides a long runway of regulated rate-base growth supporting management's >8% EPS CAGR target through 2030
Large-load contracts include customer protections (minimum-take, credit support) intended to shield existing residential/commercial ratepayers and reduce stranded-asset risk
Portfolio simplification after exiting natural gas distribution sharpens management focus and capital allocation on the core regulated electric utility
Essential-service, regulated-monopoly earnings base provides defensive, recession-resistant cash flow supporting a growing dividend
bear_case: Funding a rapidly expanding, $50+ billion multi-year capital program requires heavy and continued debt and equity issuance, risking EPS dilution, credit-metric pressure, and rising interest costs
Heavy reliance on a small number of large hyperscale customers for incremental growth creates concentration risk if AI/data-center capex spending slows or specific projects are delayed or cancelled
Aging nuclear fleet (Grand Gulf, River Bend) carries ongoing outage and regulatory risk that can remove significant baseload capacity and raise costs
Gulf Coast hurricane exposure creates lumpy, hard-to-predict storm restoration costs with regulatory lag in cost recovery

Multi-jurisdictional regulatory dependence (five+ state/city commissions plus FERC) means earnings growth is never fully in management's control, and large-load tariff/cost-allocation disputes could pressure allowed economics
